doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: An all-male college and fraternity life
summary: Fraternities taught manners and drinking politely; later changes ruined the houses.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Did the fact that it was a men’s school have an effect on your decision one way or the other?
I think it did but I didn’t realize it at the time. And I’m glad it was. It was a great experience.
And you were in a frat?

Yeah. Everybody was. In those days fraternities were very meaningful here. Eighty percent of the population was in a fraternity house. They had to have them for living, they didn’t have the dorms that they have now. And they were good institutions. They were well mannered, and each freshman would have a senior who looked after him. And for example I learned how to drink. Politely. We dressed for dinner every night. And we learned manners. And we were really well groomed. We had kids coming to this campus straight off the farm. I had a roommate like that. And boy he’s a real gentleman now. And he got that training in the fraternity houses.
Yeah. So it was an education in more ways than one.

Oh yeah. It wasn’t like the houses before — when I came back and looked at them I was disgusted. My house was so bad I wouldn’t even go near it. It was a mess. And beer cans all over the place. And what had happened was that the sophomores were living in the house because now there were girls in the dorms and the seniors and juniors wanted to be where the girls are. So there’s nobody to keep things under control in those houses. And they all went to hell, every one of them. So now we’re in better shape now. Actually the move the trustees made was a very good one I think. Very sound. Fraternities still exist, but they don’t have the houses.
